text: You already know the single-service SRE toolkit: pick the golden signals, define SLIs, set an SLO, alert on burning error budget. That model doesn't become wrong at enterprise scale, but almost everything about the environment around it changes once an organization goes from a handful of services to hundreds, owned by dozens of independently-moving teams. This lesson is about exactly what changes, and why it changes the way it does.

The first shift: a service's reliability stops being mostly a function of its own code. A checkout service with a flawless SLO can still fail users because it calls an inventory service, a pricing service, and a fraud check, each with dependencies of their own. Reliability composes down a dependency graph, and the same low-level service — an auth issuer, a feature-flag service, a shared database tier — often sits underneath dozens of unrelated call paths. That shared dependency becomes a single point of organizational blast radius, where one team's change can take down products owned by teams who've never heard of them.

That's exactly why enterprises map dependencies deliberately: knowing concretely what calls what, and which services sit on the critical path for which user outcomes, instead of treating each team's reliability as an isolated number. It's also why ad hoc, per-team conventions stop working. When there are three services, every team inventing its own SLI format is tolerable. When there are three hundred, an incident commander pulled into a 2 a.m. sev-1 needs any team's dashboard to mean the same thing — so enterprises standardize SLO formats, alert severity tied to burn rate, and runbook templates, enforced by centralized or embedded SRE teams.

That standardization gets enforced concretely through the production readiness review — a checklist-driven gate a new or changed service passes through before it earns real production traffic. It checks for exactly what this lesson has been building toward: documented SLIs and an SLO in the standard format, golden signals instrumented the standard way, known critical dependencies with a failure plan, real runbooks, and an on-call rotation that can actually answer a page. A service that can't pass that checklist isn't ready to be one node in a graph of hundreds — it's a latent incident waiting for a dependency chain to find it.

So hold onto the shape of this: dependency graphs for reasoning about blast radius, standardized SLO and alerting practice so reliability is legible across the whole org, and production readiness reviews as the gate that enforces both before launch. Next lesson builds directly on this foundation, turning the error budget you already know into something bigger — a real, enforced organizational decision-making tool, not just a dashboard number.
